text.finetune: Each run trains for 300–500 steps, at most 50 seconds on one GPU, so this tests cheap fine-tuning. It barely moves the error on what it never saw: with a family left out, 7 of 96 runs get reliably better and 0 worse; with a difficulty range left out, 1 better and 2 worse, about what chance alone gives. The best single run, 209M with LoRA tested on chaos, gets to 0.927× the original error, and every held-out set stays at 1.01–3.52× the referee. Replay is what protects normal series: without it 57 of 64 runs get worse on the 500 in-prior series (up to 1.069×); with it 0 of 128 do.
text.search:
Each method got about 2,990 Timestral calls on the 5M model per search seed. Fitness is Timestral's error divided by the referee's, with the referee required to be clearly better than "repeat last season" so the series stays forecastable. Means over search seeds:
  • CMA-ES: best series found: 123× the referee's error; reached 2× after 17 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); reached 3× after 32 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); filled 36.7 cells of the shared grid on average.
  • MAP-Elites: best series found: 218× the referee's error; reached 2× after 9 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); reached 3× after 43 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); filled 35.7 cells of the shared grid on average.
  • gradient search: best series found: 21.2× the referee's error; reached 2× after 505 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); reached 3× after 757 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); filled 5.0 cells of the shared grid on average.
  • gradient search with 12 starts: best series found: 472× the referee's error; reached 2× after 248 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); reached 3× after 718 calls on average (3 of 3 runs); filled 13.3 cells of the shared grid on average.
The charts below also show how many of the failures found on 5M still fail on the larger sizes.
